name: Seoul Dal
summary: A tethered helium balloon lifting 30 people about 130 m over Yeouido Park on a winch — nothing about it is adrenal.
description: Seoul Dal is a cable-controlled, winch-operated balloon that lifts about 30 seated passengers roughly 130 metres over Yeouido Park for around 15 minutes. name: Suwon Hwaseong
summary: A complete 18th-century city wall, 5.5 km of it, with a restored palace inside — the easiest day trip on the list by train.
description: Suwon Hwaseong is a complete UNESCO-listed fortress wall from 1796, 5.5 km around, with a town that still lives inside the gates and a restored royal palace, Hwaseong Haenggung, in the middle. Walking the full loop means a climb over Paldalsan; the flat northern stretch from Janganmun to Hwaseomun is the good part for a family that wants the view without the hill. The wall itself is free and open 24 hours; only the palace charges admission. Line 1 runs directly to Suwon Station from central Seoul, making this the simplest day trip out of the eight covered here, but budget most of a day including local transfer from the station to the wall — it is well outside the subway network the family uses at home.

name: Songdo Central Park
summary: A seawater canal through a city built from nothing in 20 years, best at dusk when the towers light up.
description: Songdo Central Park runs a 1.8 km seawater canal (with boats on it) through Incheon's planned international business district, built on reclaimed mud flats. The Tri-bowl — three inverted domes over a reflecting pool — sits at the eastern end, and a deer park and hanok village sit at the far end. It is flat and free to walk, and it is genuinely a different visit at dusk, once the surrounding towers light up, than in flat daylight. Incheon Line 1 runs directly to Central Park station.

The Tri-bowl: three inverted domes over a reflecting pool
Deer park and hanok village at the far end
tips: Arrive an hour before sunset — the park is ordinary in flat daylight and good once the towers switch on behind it.
